title: Mostly, It Is the Same Brain
author: Child Development Matters
summary: This parenting-science piece from Child Development Matters challenges the popular belief that boys and girls arrive with fundamentally different brains. It reports that, beyond overall size, a child's sex accounts for only about one per cent of the variation in brain structure, and that the two groups overlap so heavily that sex tells you almost nothing about an individual child. The author explains the mosaic finding, in which very few people are male-typical or female-typical on every measured feature. Even the small average differences are partly shaped by the different experiences children are given from day one. The piece closes by arguing the myth is not harmless, because expectations about maths or feelings quietly steer children toward what adults assume they can do. It is a useful corrective for parents deciding how to treat sons and daughters as individuals.
points: Apart from overall size, sex explains only around one per cent of the variation in children's brain structure.
Group averages describe a crowd, not the child at your kitchen table, because the two distributions overlap almost completely.
Studies across more than a thousand brains found most are a mosaic of male-typical and female-typical features rather than a matched set.
Small average differences are partly written by a world that hands boys and girls different toys, games and responses to feelings.
The myth does quiet damage by steering expectations about maths, feelings and ability, which then tend to make themselves come true.
quotes: The differences that exist are small, and most of what there is comes down to overall size, which tracks body size. Beyond size, a child's sex accounts for only around one per cent of the variation in brain structure.
The averages are real. In any one child, they are close to silent.
An average like that describes a crowd, not the child at your kitchen table.
Across well over a thousand brains, almost every one was a patchwork, some features more common in men, some more common in women, mixed together in a pattern close to unique.
A brain that spends years practising one kind of thing comes to look a little different from one that practised another.

If a girl is not wired for maths and a boy cannot really do feelings, then the maths puzzle drifts towards one child and the conversation about a hard day drifts towards another, and the expectation slowly makes itself come true.
There is no blue brain and no pink brain. There is your child, with a great deal of room to grow in any direction they are given.
